blocks.body: Hi {first_name}, I work with MDs of HVAC and M&E firms in the North who are winning plenty of work but watching the margin disappear somewhere between the tender and the final account. Usually the same three culprits: job costing in the field, retentions nobody's chasing, and the MD still in the middle of everything. I spent my career inside building services, so I know how it works in practice, not just on paper. If any of that sounds familiar, worth a quick conversation?

blocks.text: It is 7.15am and Mike is already in the van, phone wedged against his ear, talking one of the lads through a commissioning issue on a commercial fit-out in Wakefield. He has not opened his emails yet but he can feel there are twelve waiting. By 8.30 he is in the yard, signing off a materials order he probably should have delegated, fielding a question about a retention that has been sitting on the books since March, and promising the estimator he will look at the Hargreaves tender by lunchtime. He does not look at it until 4pm. The numbers look tight but the job feels winnable, so he prices it the way he always has: gut feel and a quick scan of the labour hours. At 6pm he sits at the kitchen table with the monthly P&L his accountant sends over. Revenue is up. He squints at the bottom line. It is not up anywhere near as much as the revenue suggests it should be. He is not sure which job leaked it. He has a feeling it was the Rotherham school, but he cannot prove it, and by the time it matters it is already too late to do anything about it.

We've had a decent year on paper. Turnover's up, the lads are busy, we've got work on the board into next spring. But I'm sitting here looking at this P&L and the profit just isn't where it should be. We're working harder than we ever have and I'm not taking any more home. I know some of the jobs have bled a bit but I couldn't tell you which ones or why, not properly. The accountant tells me we're doing alright but I don't feel like we're doing alright. I'm on the phone from seven in the morning and I'm still answering site queries at half seven at night. I've got good lads, don't get me wrong, but nothing moves unless I'm pushing it. I keep thinking I need to sort the pricing out, get someone else handling the day-to-day, chase up these retentions properly. I've been thinking that for about three years. I just don't know where to start, or whether spending money on getting help is going to make it worse before it gets better.

blocks.text: I spent my career inside building services: project engineer, contracts manager, then Operations Director at Harlow & Pike, where I led the HVAC division from £4.2m to £11.8m in five years. We got there by shifting from one-off installs to planned maintenance contracts and keeping a tight grip on job pricing and margin. I have lived the retentions problem, the margin bleed, and the MD-as-bottleneck problem firsthand. I now work with owners and MDs in HVAC, M&E, electrical contracting, and facilities management to fix exactly those three things, faster than they would on their own.

items: Know-how: Mike has tried an estimator, a consultant's report, and new software. None of it fixed the underlying problem because none of it came with someone who has actually run the operation. Zander has. He knows retentions, job costing, and the MD-as-bottleneck problem from the inside of building services, not from a textbook.

Speed: the engagement starts with Zander sitting in on job reviews and pricing discussions from week one. There is no six-month onboarding, no sector education required. The problems are visible quickly because Zander already speaks the language.
Ease: a weekly numbers rhythm means Mike is not left to implement a framework on his own. Zander is in the numbers with him, on live jobs, before month-end. The structure does the heavy lifting.

Fit: Zander works only with building services contractors. Mike does not need to explain what a planned maintenance contract is, how retentions work in practice, or why a job that looked winnable at tender can bleed badly in the field. That removes the biggest objection Mike has to outside help.

You are winning the work. The turnover is there. The problem is not revenue, it is that the margin disappears somewhere between the tender and the final account, and by the time the monthly P&L lands you cannot tell which job leaked it or why.

The MD answering every site call is not a people problem, it is a structure problem. Until there is a weekly operational rhythm and a management layer that actually makes decisions, the phone will keep ringing at half seven in the evening.

Retentions sitting unchased for six months is not a cash flow problem, it is a management problem. The money belongs to the business. The only reason it is still out there is that nobody owns the process of getting it back.

Bringing in an estimator, buying new software, or having a chat with the accountant does not fix margin bleed. The bleed usually happens in field job costing, not at quote stage, and you need someone who knows the difference to find it.

A contractor's MD spending nearly two grand a month on outside help needs to know the person has lived the operation, not just studied it. The fee pays for itself when one job that would have bled holds its margin instead.
